parameters.name: f0 (total proportion of potentially damageable particles)

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Periodic boundary conditions applied to the RVE edge node sets (edges a, b, c, d) per Eq. (1); reference point RP-2 fixed and RP-1 uniformly stretched along the x-axis direction (Fig. 2).
computational_details.simulation_method: Finite element method (FEM) using a 2D plane-strain representative volume element (RVE) constructed from an EBSD phase map (mapping algorithm for automatic meshing and phase assignment); element/mesh type CPE4 with a mesh size of 0.4 μm (500×500 elements). A second RVE with identical TiB2 distributions and boundary conditions but a single-phase α-ferrite matrix is used to simulate the conventional Fe-TiB steel.
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The predicted tensile response for the conventional Fe-TiB2 steel (orange curve in Fig. 11(a)) is consistent with experimental results, demonstrating the reliability of the modelling approach.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: shear-band-mediated plastic flow and particle stress shielding
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: In the FE simulation of the conventional Fe-TiB2 steel (homogeneous α-ferrite matrix), dislocation-mediated plasticity occurs predominantly through narrow shear bands oriented at ~45° to the loading axis; these patterns persist with increasing strain, leaving isolated nearly-undeformed zones (highlighted by red circles at ε = 11.0 %) caused by significant stress shielding from surrounding rigid particles, which compromises strength and ductility.

interfaces.interface_notes: TiB2 particles in the reference steel are located at grain/phase boundaries and are micron-sized; the α-ferrite/TiB2 interfaces were represented in the FE model by zero-thickness COH3D8 cohesive elements with a bilinear traction-separation law (interface stiffness K = 10^6 MPa mm^-1; interface strength Tc = 700 MPa).
interfaces.slip_behavior: Dislocation slip localises into narrow shear bands at ~45° to the loading axis within the homogeneous α-ferrite matrix (FE simulation, Fig. 12(a)); isolated stress-shielded zones remain nearly undeformed.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: This conventional Fe-TiB2 steel is the benchmark against which the newly designed low-density steel is compared: the present steel's σy (503 MPa) and σu (672 MPa) are stated to be 22 % and 30 % higher than this steel's σy (389 MPa) and σu (549 MPa), and its uniform elongation (13 %) is higher than this steel's (11 %).
comparative_performance.improvement_percentage: Present steel is 22 % (σy) and 30 % (σu) higher than this benchmark; this reference steel is correspondingly lower by the same margins. (Improvement stated on the present-steel side, as this sample is the benchmark.)

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The reference steel is described only as a 'hot-rolled monolithic ferritic steel with TiB2'; detailed thermomechanical processing parameters (temperature, passes, reduction) are not reported in the main text.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Room-temperature engineering stress-strain behaviour shown as the orange 'Fe-TiB2 steel' curve in Fig. 3(a) for comparison with the present low-density steel; detailed test conditions for the reference steel are not reported in the main text.

youngs_modulus.value: only stated as slightly higher than the present steel's 225 GPa (exact value not reported)

density.value: higher than 6.88 g cm^-3 (stated qualitatively as 'much higher' than the present steel; exact value not reported)

aliases: hot-rolled monolithic ferritic steel with TiB2

phases_present.morphology: micron-sized particles resembling those in the present steel (large primary + smaller eutectic TiB2)
phases_present.volume_fraction: ~12.5 vol.% (described as a similar volume fraction of ceramic reinforcement to the present steel)

structures.overall_structure: Homogeneous/monolithic single-phase α-ferrite matrix reinforced with micron-sized TiB2 particles (particulate metal-matrix composite); described as a 'hot-rolled monolithic ferritic steel with TiB2' with a single-phase matrix, in stark contrast to the banded dual-phase matrix of the present steel.
structures.structure_notes: The reference steel's micrograph is shown only in Supplementary Fig. S1 (not reproduced in the main text); the main text does not report its measured grain size, texture, or defect statistics.

unmapped_findings: The conventional Fe-TiB2 (reference) steel's chemical composition is not given in the main text; it is provided only in Supplementary Table S1 (as is that of the interstitial-free steel).

The specific modulus of the conventional Fe-TiB2 steel is shown in the property map (Fig. 3(c)) at approximately ~35 GPa g^-1 cm^3 (furthest right of the plotted steels), i.e. higher than the present steel's 32.7 GPa g^-1 cm^3.
The Young's modulus of the conventional Fe-TiB2 steel is stated to be slightly higher than the present steel's 225 GPa, but no numeric value is reported for the reference steel.
The conventional Fe-TiB2 steel has a higher density than the present steel's 6.88 g cm^-3 (stated only qualitatively as 'much higher'), with no numeric value reported.
In the paper's data comparison, the reference steel is labelled 'Fe-TiB2 steel' (orange) and its microstructure is shown in Supplementary Fig. S1, which is not reproduced in the main text.
The reference steel's TiB2 particles closely resemble those of the present steel, and the alloy design of the present steel does not significantly affect the solidification kinetics of TiB2.
